verdicts.reason: Agree. Facts p. 7, the only factual source in the closed universe and the government's own statement of facts, says that Nelson 'had hidden in the bushes. He opened fire as the Trailblazer approached.' It then says a rolling gun battle followed. Nothing supplied says the order of fire is disputed. Criterion 4 (+25) therefore requires a statement that contradicts the record, and it fails a careful AUSA who accepts that Nelson fired first and argues duty to retreat and preplanning. Consolidated with Opus O1.

Mostly overturned. The native instruction requires 'the final complete legal deliverable' in response2.md, says the verifier reads only that file, and tells the solver to 'Build on' response1.md. A complete supplemented brief section is therefore the requested deliverable. Restating the factual application that Kuhse's substantial-evidence framework requires is expected, not unrequested. The criteria do not exclude a permissible earlier answer; they only repeat points a complete brief would contain. Sol's separate point that criterion 3's 'only' wording compresses the record is valid at arguable, and it is consolidated with Opus O2.

Patton hanging out the window shooting is supported (Facts p. 8) and is part of the complete application.

verdicts.reason: Same ground as Sol G1, consolidated in R1. Opus's provenance point is accurate: the rubric's premise matches the assignment-1 penalty justifications and the real Eighth Circuit opinion, not the supplied Facts.

Agree. The supplied Facts show more than Nelson's 'also' firing. They also show that he hid in the bushes and fired first, that shots were fired at the Trailblazer, and that Shafer was shot in the head. A candid brief that acknowledges the ambush but argues it is legally insufficient under Kuhse may not be judged to say the 'only' evidence was that Nelson also fired. A judge may accept this framing as advocacy, so the issue is arguable.

Overturned. Opus noted that the native 'final complete legal deliverable' instruction cuts the other way. In my view it decides the question. The solver must write a complete deliverable that builds on response1.md, and the verifier reads only response2.md. An insert-only supplement is therefore not the requested deliverable. Restating the retreat facts in applying Kuhse is required, not unrequested. No permissible earlier answer is excluded.

findings.title: Criterion 4 requires saying no evidence shows who fired first, but the supplied Facts say Nelson opened fire first
findings.explanation: This consolidates Sol G1 and Opus O1. Criterion 4 (+25 of 135) credits a statement 'that there was a lack of evidence proving who fired first on May 10, 2020.' The assignment limits the solver to the uploaded Facts and Kuhse. Facts p. 7, the supervisor's own statement of facts, says that Nelson had hidden in the bushes and 'opened fire as the Trailblazer approached,' and then that 'A rolling gun battle ensued.' No supplied document says that the sequence is disputed. The criterion's premise matches the assignment-1 penalty justifications ('at a minimum, it is unclear which side fired first') and the real Eighth Circuit opinion. It does not match the record supplied here. A careful AUSA who follows the government's statement of facts, acknowledges that Nelson fired first, and argues that Patton nonetheless had a duty to retreat and acted on a plan fails this 25-point criterion. A brief that contradicts the supplied facts passes it.

findings.title: Criterion 3's 'only evidence ... is that Nelson also fired' understates the supplied record
findings.explanation: This consolidates Opus O2 and the criterion_3 part of Sol G2. Criterion 3 (+25) requires a statement that 'the only evidence of self-defense is that Nelson also fired a gun.' The supplied Facts show more. Nelson hid in the bushes and opened fire first as the Trailblazer approached, shots were fired at the Trailblazer, and Shafer was shot in the head during the shootout. Reducing that evidence to Nelson having 'also' fired is advocacy framing that a judge may accept, particularly if a brief argues that Nelson's gunfire is the only evidence offered for self-defense. A candid brief that acknowledges the ambush and first fire, and argues that the evidence is still insufficient under Kuhse because of the duty to retreat and preplanning, may be judged not to say that the 'only' evidence was that Nelson also fired. The issue is therefore arguable.
